## Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/toolik_weather.csv'
toolik = pd.read_csv(url)
```

## Part 1: Vital statistics

**1. How many rows and how many columns does the dataset have?**

```{python}
toolik.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**11,171 rows and 21 columns.** One row per day. Hold on to the row count, because several of the
later questions compare a column's count against it: 11,171 is what "complete" looks like in this
file, and any count below it is a gap somewhere.
:::

**2. What are the column names? Get them as a Python list.**

```{python}
toolik.columns.tolist()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Twenty-one names, and they fall into three groups. Three columns are time labels (`Year`,
`Month`, `Date`), two more identify the site (`LTER_Site`, `Station`), and the remaining sixteen
are nine measurements, six `Flag_` columns and `Comments`. Each flag column sits immediately after
the measurement it annotates, which makes the list look at a glance like a neat alternation of
measurement, flag, measurement, flag. Nine and six do not pair up, though, and three of the
measurements have no flag column at all: `Daily_Windspeed_AbsMax_m_s`, `Moss` and `Soil20cm`.

Two details in the spelling are worth writing down while the list is on screen. First, the flag
prefix is `Flag_` on four columns and `FLAG_` on two, and Python string matching is case
sensitive, so any attempt to select "all the flag columns" by name has to account for both
spellings. Second, `FLAG_Daily_globalrad_total_mjm2` sits directly after a measurement column
named `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2`, which is megajoules per square metre against joules per
square centimetre. No column in this file is called `Daily_globalrad_total_mjm2`, and the
radiation values run into the low thousands, which is an ordinary daily total in J/cm² and an
impossible one in MJ/m², so the flag name is probably the one nobody updated. Noticing a
mismatch like that from the column names alone is most of what today's practice is for!
:::

**3. What is the data type of each column?**

```{python}
toolik.dtypes
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Three `int64` columns, nine `float64`, and nine `object`.** The nine object columns are the
site and station labels, the six flag columns and `Comments`, all of which hold text.

The column to look at twice is **`Date`, which pandas has stored as `int64`, not as a date.** The
file writes 1 June 1988 as `19880601`, which is a perfectly valid integer, so `read_csv` took it
as a number. Storing a date that way means you can add 1 to it and get `19880602` by luck, then
add 31 to `19880601` and get `19880632`, which is not a day at all. Nothing here is broken, but
until we convert the column properly on Day 6, treat it as a label rather than as a date.
:::

**4. Yesterday's practice told you this record runs from June 1988 to December 2018. Do not take
that on trust. Use `.min()` and `.max()` on the `Date` column to find the exact first and last
day, and say which cell is your evidence.**

```{python}
toolik.describe()
```

```{python}
toolik['Date'].min()
```

```{python}
toolik['Date'].max()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**The record runs from 1 June 1988 to 31 December 2018.** The two cells above are the evidence:
they print `19880601` and `20181231`.

Yesterday's page was right, and checking it was still worth doing. "June 1988" and "1 June 1988"
are different claims, and only one of them is in the file. Repeating what another page told you
is not evidence, which is why today's practice asks for a cell underneath every sentence you
write.

Read the two numbers rather than the `min` and `max` rows of `.describe()`. `Date` is stored as an
integer, so `.describe()` also reports a mean and a standard deviation for it, and neither of
those means anything: the average of `19880601` and `20181231` is not a day.

Beginning on 1 June rather than 1 January leaves 1988 a partial year in this file, which
question 10 takes up in more detail.

The `count` row of the `.describe()` you ran back in Part 1 is worth a second look while you are
here, read across the columns rather than down one: `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C` has all 11,171
values, but `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2` has only 4,118.
:::

## Part 2: The health check

**5. Run `.info()`. How many columns have fewer non-null values than there are rows?**

```{python}
toolik.info()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**15 of the 21 columns.** Only six columns are complete at 11,171 values: `Year`, `Month`,
`Date`, `LTER_Site`, `Station` and `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C`. Every other column, including every
measurement other than the mean air temperature, has gaps somewhere.

One piece of good news: `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C`, the column yesterday's whole workflow was built
on, is the only measurement in the file with no missing values at all.
:::

**6. Use `.isnull().sum()` to count missing values per column. Which three columns are the
emptiest?**

```{python}
toolik.isnull().sum()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**`FLAG_Daily_windsp_mean_msec` (11,170 missing), `FLAG_Daily_globalrad_total_mjm2` (11,156) and
`Flag_Daily_AirTemp_AbsMax_C` (10,151).** The three emptiest columns are all flag columns, and so
are the next three: every one of the six flag columns is missing more than 8,000 of its 11,171
values. The emptiest two columns that are not flags are `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2`, with 7,053
missing, and `Comments`, with 2,247.

Finding those three takes a little reading, because `.isnull().sum()` prints the columns in the
order they appear in the file rather than in order of emptiness, so the six flag columns are
scattered down the list next to the measurements they annotate. Chaining
`.sort_values(ascending=False)` on the end will rank them for you, which is worth doing on a
wider file than this one.

However you get there, all six flag columns come out emptier than any measurement in the file,
and the gap is a hint rather than an alarm: a flag column is only filled in on the days when
something about the reading was worth writing down, so a nearly-empty one is a column doing
exactly its job.
:::

**7. One of the flag columns is empty in all but a very small number of rows. Which one, and how
many values does it actually have?**

```{python}
toolik.notnull().sum().sort_values()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**`FLAG_Daily_windsp_mean_msec`, which is missing in 11,170 of 11,171 rows and therefore holds
exactly one value.** The next emptiest column, `FLAG_Daily_globalrad_total_mjm2`, holds 15.

A flag column is an annotation, not a measurement. It is there to mark the days on which
something was unusual about the reading, and on an ordinary day there is nothing to say, so the
cell is left empty. An almost-empty flag column means almost every wind speed reading was
routine. A full flag column would be the alarming result!

The practical consequence is that emptiness alone is not a quality score. `Comments` is 20%
empty and `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2` is 63% empty, and those two nulls mean completely
different things: one is a note nobody needed to write, the other is a measurement nobody made.
:::

## Part 3: What varies, and what doesn't

**8. Use `.value_counts()` on `LTER_Site` and on `Station`. What does each column tell you?**

```{python}
toolik['LTER_Site'].value_counts()
```

```{python}
toolik['Station'].value_counts()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Neither column varies, so neither one can tell you anything about the differences between
rows.** `LTER_Site` is `ARC` in all 11,171 rows and `Station` is `TLKMAIN` in all 11,171 rows. A
column with one distinct value cannot distinguish one row from another, so it can never explain
anything, and grouping by it would return a single group.

They still have a use, though. They record **provenance**: every row came from the main
meteorological station at the Arctic LTER site, so this whole file is one instrument at one
place. Provenance is worth a sentence in your biography, because it settles two questions at
once. Nothing here needs to be averaged across stations, and these data describe one point on
the North Slope rather than the Arctic in general.
:::

**9. Use `.value_counts()` on `Flag_Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C`. What values appear, and what do you
think they mean?**

```{python}
toolik['Flag_Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].value_counts()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**One value appears, `E`, on 1,310 days.** In the Arctic LTER flag convention, `E` marks a value
that was **estimated** rather than measured directly, usually filled in from a nearby sensor by
regression when the main logger failed. The `Comments` column says so in words on those rows,
with entries such as "Air temp 1 & 5 meter estimated from regression".

Question 5 found `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C` to be the one measurement with no missing values, which
made it look like the most trustworthy column in the file. Put the two results together and the
picture changes: 1,310 of those 11,171 values, or 11.7%, are flagged as estimated. The column is
complete because somebody filled the gaps, not because the instrument never stopped. Counting
nulls would never have shown you this, and it is worth knowing before you compute a temperature
trend from the column.

Note also that `.value_counts()` drops nulls by default, which is why the 9,861 unflagged days
do not appear. Use `.value_counts(dropna=False)` when you want to see them.
:::

**10. Use `.value_counts()` on the `Year` column and look at both ends of the result, with
`.head()` and then with `.tail()`. Do all years have the same number of observations? What would
explain a year with fewer?**

```{python}
toolik['Year'].value_counts().head()
```

```{python}
toolik['Year'].value_counts().tail()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**No, and the two ends of the result show you two different things.** `.value_counts()` sorts by
count from largest to smallest, so `.head()` returns five years with 366 rows each. Seven years in
this file have 366 rows, because seven of them are leap years, and every other full year has 365.
Five of those seven tie for the top of the list, so which five you see, and in what order, depends
on how pandas breaks the tie. Your list may not match the one printed above, which is fine and
expected! `.tail()` returns the other end of the same list, and the short year sits down there:
**1988 has 214 rows.**

The question asks for both ends because a list sorted by count puts each year wherever its count
happens to fall, so a year with fewer observations than its neighbours sorts to the bottom and is
invisible from the top. Whenever you use `.value_counts()` to check whether groups are the same
size, read both ends of it.

The 214 days are the start of the record rather than a gap in the middle of a year. Counting
back 214 days from 31 December 1988 reaches 1 June, which agrees with the `Date` minimum of
`19880601` you saw in question 4. Toolik began recording in mid-year.

The consequence is a real one. Any per-year summary you compute for 1988 covers June to December
only, so it leaves out the coldest five months and will not be comparable with any other year in
the file. Whenever a group has fewer rows than its neighbours, find out which rows are missing
before you compare the groups.
:::

## Part 4: The numbers

**11. What is the mean daily air temperature across the whole record? The minimum? The maximum?**

```{python}
toolik['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].describe()
```

**12. Are the mean, the minimum and the maximum plausible for a site above the Arctic Circle?
Say why or why not.**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Mean -8.20 °C, minimum -55.60 °C, maximum 20.70 °C, over all 11,171 days**, with a standard
deviation of 14.83 °C and a median of -7.10 °C.

All three numbers are plausible for the North Slope of Alaska. A mean well below freezing is what
makes this a permafrost site. The extremes are extremes of a *daily mean*, not of an
instantaneous reading, so -55.6 °C is a day that averaged -55.6 °C, which is a good deal more
remarkable than a brief cold spike. The quartiles are the useful check on plausibility: 25% of
days average below -19.7 °C and 75% are below 4.4 °C, so this is a place that spends most of the
year frozen and thaws briefly.

One caution about the mean. It is the average of every day in the file, and the file starts on
1 June 1988, so the first year contributes a summer and no winter. The effect is small here,
-8.26 °C if you exclude 1988 entirely against -8.20 °C with it, but the direction is predictable:
an unbalanced record pulls the average toward whatever season is over-represented.
:::

**13. Pick one other numeric column and report its range. Does anything about it look wrong?**

```{python}
toolik[['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C', 'Daily_Precip_Total_mm', 'Daily_windsp_mean_msec']].describe()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**`Daily_Precip_Total_mm` runs from 0 to 64.5 mm, with a mean of 0.95 mm.** Nothing in that
range is physically impossible. The `count` is the problem: **10,751**, which is 420 days short
of the 11,171 in the file, and those absences are not spread evenly. They fall in six years,
mostly in 1995 (183 missing days), 1994 (92), 1990 (88) and 2004 (52), with the last five days
split between 1989 and 1993. So 1995 reports precipitation on 182 days out of 365, and any
annual rainfall total for that year would be roughly half a year of rain presented as a whole
one.

The trap is that a missing day and a dry day look the same once they are summed. The median
precipitation is 0.0 mm, because 7,278 of the recorded days had no rain at all, so a missing day
quietly resembles the most common real value. Reporting the mean of 0.95 mm is safe, because
pandas divides by the days it actually has, but any `.sum()` over this column will undercount
without warning you.

`Daily_windsp_mean_msec` shows the same pattern more mildly: 0 to 12.5 m/s over 10,345 days, so
826 days have no wind reading. If you looked at `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2` instead, its
minimum of -2.0 J/cm² is genuinely impossible, because a day cannot receive negative sunlight,
and that single value is a good example of an error that only a physical sanity check will
catch.
:::

## Part 5: A tidier table

**14. Build a list of the five columns you'd keep if you had to hand this dataset to a
colleague who only cared about temperature. Use it to make a smaller DataFrame.**

```{python}
temp_columns = ['Year', 'Month', 'Date', 'Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C', 'Daily_AirTemp_AbsMin_C']
toolik_temps = toolik[temp_columns]
toolik_temps.head()
```

**15. Build a dictionary that renames at least two of those columns to something shorter
and clearer. Apply it with `.rename(columns=...)` and confirm the new names.**

```{python}
shorter = {
    'Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C': 'temp_mean_c',
    'Daily_AirTemp_AbsMin_C': 'temp_min_c',
}
toolik_temps = toolik_temps.rename(columns=shorter)
toolik_temps.columns.tolist()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Two Day 2 collections doing two different jobs. The **list** is an ordered selection: passing it
to `toolik[...]` returns the columns in the order you wrote them, so the list decides both what
is kept and how it is arranged. The **dictionary** is a lookup from old name to new name, and
because it is a mapping rather than a sequence, its order is irrelevant and it may name only
some of the columns. Anything not mentioned as a key keeps its current name.

Two things to check in your own version. First, keeping the time columns matters: a table of
temperatures with no `Year`, `Month` or `Date` cannot be plotted against time, so the useful
five columns are three labels and two measurements. Second, `.rename()` returns a **new**
DataFrame and does not alter the original, which is why the code reassigns `toolik_temps`.
Confirm this by running `toolik.columns.tolist()` again: the full table still has
`Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C` under its original name. Keeping units in the new names, as `temp_mean_c`
does, is worth the two extra characters.
:::

## Part 6: Write the biography

There is no single right answer here. A strong biography states a number for every claim, names
at least one problem that the file does not announce, and gives a fitness-for-purpose verdict
with a condition attached rather than an unqualified yes. Here is one that would earn full marks.

:::{.callout-note title="✅ A model answer"}
This file holds daily weather from the main meteorological station (`TLKMAIN`) at Toolik Field
Station, part of the Arctic LTER site (`ARC`) on the North Slope of Alaska. Both identifier
columns hold a single value throughout, so every observation comes from one instrument cluster
at one place. The 21 columns cover nine measurements: air temperature (daily mean, absolute
maximum, absolute minimum), precipitation, mean and maximum wind speed, global radiation, and
moss and 20 cm soil temperature. Six of the nine have a flag column.

Coverage is 11,171 daily rows from 1 June 1988 to 31 December 2018, with every calendar day
present. 1988 holds only 214 rows because the record starts in June, so it is a partial year,
not a lost one.

Fifteen of the 21 columns have missing values. Daily mean air temperature, complete at 11,171
values, is the column I would trust most. I would not trust global radiation, which has 4,118
values and includes an impossible -2.0 J/cm², or annual precipitation totals, because 420 days
are absent and 183 of them fall in 1995 alone.

Two cautions. First, `Date` is stored as the integer 19880601, not as a date, so it cannot be
sorted or differenced as a date until converted. Second, the complete temperature column is not
fully measured: 1,310 days, 11.7% of the record, have an `E` flag meaning the value was
estimated from a nearby sensor.

Could this describe change in Arctic summer temperatures since 1988? Yes, with one check first.
All 31 years have complete June to August coverage and no missing means, but 85 of the 92 summer
days in 1988 are flagged estimated, and no summer day after 2006 has a flag. Because 1988
anchors any trend, I would confirm the result holds with those days excluded.
:::

### The optional loop

The Field Note offered a loop as a shortcut for checking several columns at once. Running it on
the two columns in the example prints the missing-value count for each, which is the same pair of
numbers you would get from two separate calls:

```{python}
for column_name in ['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C', 'Daily_Precip_Total_mm']:
    print(column_name, toolik[column_name].isnull().sum())
```

Anyone who worked one column at a time has lost nothing. The loop saves typing, not insight.

## Where the marks are

If you compare your notebook against this key, look for these four things before you look at
anything else.

1. **Every factual claim in your biography has a code cell above it that produced it.** A
   sentence such as "the record covers about thirty years" is the failure mode this exercise is
   built to catch. "1 June 1988 to 31 December 2018, 11,171 daily rows" is the pass.
2. **You found 1988 and explained it.** Reporting that 1988 has 214 rows is half the answer. The
   mark is for saying why: the record begins on 1 June 1988, so 1988 is a partial year rather
   than a year with days missing from it, and no per-year figure for 1988 is comparable with any
   other year in the file.
3. **You read the flag columns as part of the file's design rather than as errors,** and you
   connected them back to `Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C`. The column with no missing values contains
   1,310 estimated ones, and a biography that reports it as complete without mentioning the
   flags sends its reader off with the wrong idea of how solid the temperature record is.
4. **Your answers say what a number means rather than what it is.** "420 values are missing from
   precipitation" restates the output. "420 missing days, 183 of them in 1995, so an annual total
   for that year covers half a year of rain" reads it.
